claim: Enalapril is a drug widely prescribed for hypertension.
source: In this study, using IMR90 cells and aged mice, we revealed that enalapril, a drug widely prescribed for hypertension, can improve both cellular senescence and individual health.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as established knowledge about enalapril's clinical use.

claim: Enalapril can improve both cellular senescence and individual health in IMR90 cells and aged mice.
source: In this study, using IMR90 cells and aged mice, we revealed that enalapril, a drug widely prescribed for hypertension, can improve both cellular senescence and individual health.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from cell culture and mouse models.

claim: Phosphorylated Smad1/5/9 act as pivotal mediators of the anti-senescence properties of enalapril.
source: Mechanistically, phosphorylated Smad1/5/9 act as pivotal mediators of the anti-senescence properties of enalapril.
evidence: This mechanistic finding is supported by experimental data including Western blots, CUT&Tag analysis, and functional studies with inhibitors.

claim: Enalapril stimulates downstream genes involved in cell cycle regulation and antioxidative defenses.
source: It stimulates downstream genes involved in cell cycle regulation and antioxidative defenses, facilitating cell proliferation and diminishing the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), thus increasing the antioxidative ability of enalapril.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data, CUT&Tag analysis, and RT-qPCR measurements showing gene expression changes.

claim: Enalapril facilitates cell proliferation.
source: It stimulates downstream genes involved in cell cycle regulation and antioxidative defenses, facilitating cell proliferation and diminishing the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), thus increasing the antioxidative ability of enalapril.
evidence: This is supported by Ki67 staining data and growth curve measurements showing increased cell proliferation.

claim: Enalapril diminishes the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: It stimulates downstream genes involved in cell cycle regulation and antioxidative defenses, facilitating cell proliferation and diminishing the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), thus increasing the antioxidative ability of enalapril.
evidence: This is supported by DCFH-DA probe measurements showing reduced ROS fluorescence levels after enalapril treatment.

claim: Enalapril enhances memory capacity in aged mice.
source: At the organismal level, enalapril has been shown to bolster the physiological performance of various organs; it notably enhances memory capacity and renal function and relieves lipid accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by Y-maze behavioral test data showing increased spontaneous alternation rates.

claim: Enalapril enhances renal function in aged mice.
source: At the organismal level, enalapril has been shown to bolster the physiological performance of various organs; it notably enhances memory capacity and renal function and relieves lipid accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by serum creatinine measurements and Sirius red staining showing reduced kidney fibrosis.

claim: Enalapril relieves lipid accumulation in aged mice.
source: At the organismal level, enalapril has been shown to bolster the physiological performance of various organs; it notably enhances memory capacity and renal function and relieves lipid accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by Oil Red O staining and serum lipid measurements showing reduced triglycerides and LDL.

claim: Aging is a significant risk factor for many chronic diseases.
source: Geroscience is a burgeoning field of study in which researchers hypothesize that aging is a significant risk factor for many chronic diseases.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kirkland, 2016 and López-Otín et al., 2023.

claim: Interventions targeting the mechanisms of aging might delay the onset or slow the progression of chronic diseases.
source: These findings suggest that interventions targeting the mechanisms of aging might delay the onset or slow the progression of these diseases (Kirkland, 2016; López-Otín et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kirkland, 2016 and López-Otín et al., 2023.

claim: Cellular senescence is a pivotal indicator of aging.
source: Cellular senescence, a pivotal indicator of aging, is characterized by irreversible cell cycle arrest triggered by cellular damage or stress (Khosla et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Khosla et al., 2020 and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: Cellular senescence is characterized by irreversible cell cycle arrest triggered by cellular damage or stress.
source: Cellular senescence, a pivotal indicator of aging, is characterized by irreversible cell cycle arrest triggered by cellular damage or stress (Khosla et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Khosla et al., 2020 and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: Senescent cells exhibit increased activity of the lysosomal enzyme senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal).
source: During cellular senescence, cells exhibit increased activity of the lysosomal enzyme senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal), decreased proliferation marker Ki67 signals and increased senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) secretion (Coppé et al., 2008; Dimri et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Coppé et al., 2008 and Dimri et al., 1995.

claim: Senescent cells exhibit decreased proliferation marker Ki67 signals.
source: During cellular senescence, cells exhibit increased activity of the lysosomal enzyme senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal), decreased proliferation marker Ki67 signals and increased senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) secretion (Coppé et al., 2008; Dimri et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Coppé et al., 2008 and Dimri et al., 1995.

claim: Senescent cells exhibit increased senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) secretion.
source: During cellular senescence, cells exhibit increased activity of the lysosomal enzyme senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal), decreased proliferation marker Ki67 signals and increased senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) secretion (Coppé et al., 2008; Dimri et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Coppé et al., 2008 and Dimri et al., 1995.

claim: The activation of tumor suppressor pathways, such as p16INK4a/RB, is essential for senescence-related cessation of proliferation.
source: Currently, the activation of tumor suppressor pathways, such as p16INK4a/RB, is deemed essential for senescence-related cessation of proliferation (Baker et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baker et al., 2011.

claim: The expression of p16 is suppressed by inhibitor of DNA-binding (ID) proteins.
source: Researchers have suggested that the expression of p16 is suppressed by inhibitor of DNA-binding (ID) proteins.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the context.

claim: The expression of the ID1 gene is downregulated by transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β).
source: The expression of the ID1 gene is downregulated by transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β), while it is upregulated by BMP-mediated phosphorylated SMAD signaling in various cell types (Hayashi et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hayashi et al., 2016 and Liang et al., 2009.

claim: The expression of the ID1 gene is upregulated by BMP-mediated phosphorylated SMAD signaling in various cell types.
source: The expression of the ID1 gene is downregulated by transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β), while it is upregulated by BMP-mediated phosphorylated SMAD signaling in various cell types (Hayashi et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hayashi et al., 2016 and Liang et al., 2009.

claim: SMADs are crucial transcriptional effector factors responsible for transmitting TGF-β/BMP signals.
source: SMADs are crucial transcriptional effector factors responsible for transmitting TGF-β/BMP signals (Urist, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Urist, 1965 and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: The BMP-SMAD signaling pathway can modulate genes involved in the cell cycle, which affects the balance between cell proliferation and senescence.
source: Numerous studies have shown that the BMP-SMAD signaling pathway can modulate genes involved in the cell cycle, which affects the balance between cell proliferation and senescence (Genander et al., 2014; Hayashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Genander et al., 2014 and Hayashi et al., 2016.

claim: Phosphorylated SMAD plays a crucial role in the induction and maintenance of pluripotency.
source: Phosphorylated SMAD plays a crucial role in the induction and maintenance of pluripotency, helping maintain tissue homeostasis during aging (Orlowski, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Orlowski, 2017.

claim: Dysregulation of BMP signaling during aging can lead to fibrosis, impaired wound healing, or excessive tissue calcification.
source: However, dysregulation of BMP signaling during aging can lead to fibrosis, impaired wound healing, or excessive tissue calcification, which are detrimental to tissue function (Lyu et al., 2018; Rahman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lyu et al., 2018 and Rahman et al., 2015.

claim: Specific senolytic drugs, such as dasatinib and quercetin, can eliminate senescent cells, reverse aging phenotypes, and increase the survival rate of mice.
source: Research has proven that specific senolytic drugs, such as dasatinib and quercetin, can eliminate senescent cells, reverse aging phenotypes, and increase the survival rate of mice (Xu et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xu et al., 2018 and Zhu et al., 2015.

claim: Current senolytics are not universally effective across different cell types and display inconsistent sensitivities.
source: However, the current senolytics are not universally effective across different cell types and display inconsistent sensitivities, thereby limiting their broad application (Yousefzadeh et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yousefzadeh et al., 2018 and Zhu et al., 2016.

claim: Metformin and rapamycin have shown promise in reducing aging phenotypes and extending the lifespan.
source: For example, drugs such as metformin, which is typically used to treat type 2 diabetes, and rapamycin, an immunosuppressant, have shown promise in reducing aging phenotypes and extending the lifespan (Bharath et al., 2020; Harrison et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bharath et al., 2020 and Harrison et al., 2009.

claim: Long-term-cultured IMR90 cells present a characteristic senescence phenotype, characterized by increased SA-β-gal staining, increased expression of p16 and p21, and reduced expression of Ki67.
source: Compared with young cells, long-term-cultured IMR90 cells presented a characteristic senescence phenotype, characterized by increased SA-β-gal staining, increased expression of the cell cycle arrest factors p16 and p21, and reduced expression of the proliferation marker Ki67 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C including SA-β-gal staining, Western blots, and Ki67 immunofluorescence.

claim: The release of SASP factors including IL1β, IL6, and CXCL10 increases with the degree of senescence in IMR90 cells.
source: Additionally, the release of SASP factors that significantly alter the cellular microenvironment, including the well-described factors IL1β, IL6, and CXCL10, has also been reported to increase the degree of senescence (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Enalapril treatment at various concentrations reduced SA-β-gal staining in IMR90 cells.
source: Notably, enalapril treatment at various concentrations reduced SA-β-gal staining, and increased Ki67 positivity in IMR90 cells (Figure 1A, B, D and E).
evidence: This is supported by SA-β-gal staining data shown in Figure 1A and quantification in Figure 1D.

claim: Enalapril treatment increased Ki67 positivity in IMR90 cells.
source: Notably, enalapril treatment at various concentrations reduced SA-β-gal staining, and increased Ki67 positivity in IMR90 cells (Figure 1A, B, D and E).
evidence: This is supported by Ki67 immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B and quantification in Figure 1E.

claim: Western blot analysis confirmed a decrease in the senescence markers p16 and p21 with the optimal effect of 10 μM enalapril.
source: Western blot analysis confirmed a decrease in the senescence markers p16 and p21 with the optimal effect of 10 μM enalapril (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The expression of SASP genes decreased significantly after enalapril treatment.
source: In general, we found that the expression of SASP genes decreased significantly (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in the heatmap in Figure 1F.

claim: The expression of cell cycle arrest factors decreased after exposure to enalapril.
source: The expression of cell cycle arrest factors typically increased during senescence; however, the expression of these factors decreased after exposure to enalapril, whereas the expression of cell cycle genes related to cell proliferation increased upon treatment with enalapril at the optimal concentration of 10 μM (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in the heatmap in Figure 1F.

claim: The expression of cell cycle genes related to cell proliferation increased upon treatment with enalapril at the optimal concentration of 10 μM.
source: The expression of cell cycle arrest factors typically increased during senescence; however, the expression of these factors decreased after exposure to enalapril, whereas the expression of cell cycle genes related to cell proliferation increased upon treatment with enalapril at the optimal concentration of 10 μM (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in the heatmap in Figure 1F.

claim: Enalapril treatment significantly reduced the expression of prominent SASP genes such as IL1β and IL6.
source: We, therefore, treated the cells with 10 μM enalapril via RT-qPCR and detected that many prominent SASP genes, such as IL1β and IL6, were significantly reduced compared with those in the control (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Enalapril treatment increased the cell growth rate and delayed the transition to the growth arrest phase.
source: Moreover, enalapril treatment increased the cell growth rate and delayed the transition to the growth arrest phase (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Enalapril notably elevated the phosphorylation level of Smad1/5/9 without affecting Smad2/3 phosphorylation.
source: We found that enalapril notably elevated the phosphorylation level of Smad1/5/9 without affecting Smad2/3 phosphorylation, effectively reversing the decline of pSmad1/5/9 levels in senescent cells, suggesting a possible role for the BMP-pSmad1/5/9 pathway (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Enalapril effectively reverses the decline of pSmad1/5/9 levels in senescent cells.
source: We found that enalapril notably elevated the phosphorylation level of Smad1/5/9 without affecting Smad2/3 phosphorylation, effectively reversing the decline of pSmad1/5/9 levels in senescent cells, suggesting a possible role for the BMP-pSmad1/5/9 pathway (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: GSEA confirmed that enalapril treatment increased BMP signaling.
source: To validate the pathway alterations in the gene expression profile, GSEA confirmed that enalapril treatment increased BMP signaling (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The level of the Smad4 protein increased after enalapril treatment.
source: Concurrently, the level of the Smad4 protein, which is required for pSmad1/5/9 to enter the nucleus, also increased, suggesting that enalapril might facilitate the nuclear entry of pSmad1/5/9 and modulate downstream genes (Figure 2A; Guglielmi et al., 2021; Senft et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A and citations to Guglielmi et al., 2021 and Senft et al., 2019.

claim: Smad4 is required for pSmad1/5/9 to enter the nucleus.
source: Concurrently, the level of the Smad4 protein, which is required for pSmad1/5/9 to enter the nucleus, also increased, suggesting that enalapril might facilitate the nuclear entry of pSmad1/5/9 and modulate downstream genes (Figure 2A; Guglielmi et al., 2021; Senft et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guglielmi et al., 2021 and Senft et al., 2019.

claim: The expression of Smad4 was reduced in senescent cells.
source: Notably, the expression of Smad4 was reduced in senescent cells, supporting the notion that enalapril reverses senescence-associated defects in BMP signaling (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Enalapril treatment increased the pSmad1/5/9 binding signals at the transcription start site (TSS) regions.
source: To further assess the impact on gene regulation, we employed CUT&Tag analysis of pSmad1/5/9 and found that enalapril treatment increased the pSmad1/5/9 binding signals at the transcription start site (TSS) regions (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by CUT&Tag data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: BMP4 increased pSmad5 levels.
source: Our findings revealed that BMP4 increased pSmad5 levels, which correlated with decreased p16 and p21, reduced β-gal staining and increased Ki67 positivity, indicating a mitigated senescent phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: BMP4 treatment correlated with decreased p16 and p21, reduced β-gal staining and increased Ki67 positivity.
source: Our findings revealed that BMP4 increased pSmad5 levels, which correlated with decreased p16 and p21, reduced β-gal staining and increased Ki67 positivity, indicating a mitigated senescent phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: Treatment with the BMP receptor inhibitor LDN or BMPR1A knockdown reversed the changes in pSmad1/5/9 levels and senescence markers.
source: In contrast, when cells were treated with the BMP receptor inhibitor LDN or subjected to BMPR1A knockdown, the changes in pSmad1/5/9 levels and senescence markers were completely reversed, highlighting that the suppression of pSmad1/5/9 accelerates the progression of senescence (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The suppression of pSmad1/5/9 accelerates the progression of senescence.
source: In contrast, when cells were treated with the BMP receptor inhibitor LDN or subjected to BMPR1A knockdown, the changes in pSmad1/5/9 levels and senescence markers were completely reversed, highlighting that the suppression of pSmad1/5/9 accelerates the progression of senescence (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: LDN upregulated SASP genes and downregulated cell cycle genes.
source: RNA-seq analysis revealed that LDN upregulated SASP genes and downregulated cell cycle genes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The subsequent addition of enalapril did not reverse the changes induced by LDN, suggesting that the anti-senescence function of enalapril relies on pSmad1/5/9.
source: On the basis of these findings, the subsequent addition of enalapril did not reverse these changes, which suggests that the anti-senescence function of enalapril relies on pSmad1/5/9 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2D and represents an inference from the experimental results.

claim: In the presence of LDN, neither enalapril nor BMP4 restored Smad1/5/9 phosphorylation or the expression of p16 and p21.
source: Furthermore, western blot results also revealed that in the presence of LDN, neither enalapril nor BMP4 restored Smad1/5/9 phosphorylation or the expression of p16 and p21 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Enalapril failed to counteract the senescence-promoting effects induced by either LDN treatment or BMPR1A knockdown.
source: Similarly, β-gal and Ki67 staining also revealed that enalapril failed to counteract the senescence-promoting effects induced by either LDN treatment or BMPR1A knockdown (Figure 2F and G, Figure 2—figure supplement 3F, G).
evidence: This is supported by β-gal and Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 2F, G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3F, G.

claim: The ID family is recognized as a key downstream target of pSmad1/5/9.
source: The ID family, which is recognized as a key downstream target of pSmad1/5/9, serves as a biomarker for Smad1/5/9 phosphorylation levels (Genander et al., 2014; Hayashi et al., 2016; Ramachandran et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2022; Ying et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Genander et al., 2014; Hayashi et al., 2016; Ramachandran et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2022; Ying et al., 2003.

claim: ID1 was the top-ranked transcription factor that pSmad1/5/9 bound to its promoter region after enalapril treatment.
source: Coincidentally, we found that ID1 was the top-ranked transcription factor that pSmad1/5/9 bound to its promoter region via CUT&Tag analysis after enalapril treatment (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by CUT&Tag analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Enalapril significantly increased pSmad1/5/9 enrichment at the ID1 promoter.
source: Moreover, IGV analysis confirmed that enalapril significantly increased pSmad1/5/9 enrichment at the ID1 promoter (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by IGV analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The expression levels of both ID1 and ID2 were elevated after enalapril treatment.
source: Simultaneously, the expression levels of both ID1 and ID2 were elevated (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Inhibiting pSmad1/5/9 with LDN or shRNA targeting BMPR1A led to decreased ID1 and ID2 levels.
source: Conversely, inhibiting pSmad1/5/9 with LDN or shRNA targeting BMPR1A led to decreased ID1 and ID2 levels, confirming the regulatory link between pSmad1/5/9 and the ID family (Figure 3E, Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The ID family can suppress p16 and p21 expression, thus inhibiting cell cycle arrest and delaying cellular senescence.
source: Prior studies have indicated that the ID family can suppress p16 and p21 expression, thus inhibiting cell cycle arrest and delaying cellular senescence (Hayashi et al., 2016; Lyden et al., 1999; Ying et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hayashi et al., 2016; Lyden et al., 1999; Ying et al., 2003.

claim: ID1 and ID2 levels decrease during senescence.
source: This prompted us to examine ID protein expression during senescence, where we observed a decrease in ID1 and ID2 levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The knockdown of ID1 and ID2 via shRNA or an ID1 inhibitor resulted in a significant increase in p16 and p21 expression.
source: The knockdown of ID1 and ID2 via shRNA or an ID1 inhibitor resulted in a decreasing trend of ID1 or ID2 expression and a significant increase in p16 and p21 expression (Figure 3F, I).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3F and I.

claim: β-gal increased the proportion of positively stained cells after the knockdown of ID1 or ID2.
source: In addition, while β-gal increased the proportion of positively stained cells, the Ki67 proliferation signal decreased nearly fourfold after the knockdown of ID1 or ID2, resembling the changes observed during senescence (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is supported by SA-β-gal staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The Ki67 proliferation signal decreased nearly fourfold after the knockdown of ID1 or ID2.
source: In addition, while β-gal increased the proportion of positively stained cells, the Ki67 proliferation signal decreased nearly fourfold after the knockdown of ID1 or ID2, resembling the changes observed during senescence (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is supported by Ki67 immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The expression of traditional SASP factors, such as IL1β and IL6, significantly increased after ID knockdown.
source: Indeed, the expression of traditional SASP factors, such as IL1β and IL6, which decrease with enalapril treatment, significantly increased after ID knockdown (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: ID knockdown did not affect pSmad1/5/9 levels, confirming that ID is a downstream effector of pSmad1/5/9.
source: Importantly, ID knockdown did not affect pSmad1/5/9 levels, confirming that ID is a downstream effector of pSmad1/5/9, influencing the expression of genes such as p16, p21, and SASP-related genes (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3J and represents an inference from the experimental results.

claim: The continued addition of enalapril to ID-knockdown cells did not significantly alter β-gal or Ki67 signals compared with those in the ID-knockdown group without enalapril.
source: The continued addition of enalapril to these ID-knockdown cells did not significantly alter β-gal or Ki67 signals compared with those in the ID-knockdown group without enalapril, implying that the benefits of enalapril may be ID dependent (Figure 3K–L, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by β-gal and Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 3K-L and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Enalapril treatment led to enrichment of pSmad1/5/9 in the GO pathway associated with DNA replication, the cell cycle, and the oxidative stress response.
source: Analysis of CUT&Tag-upregulated peaks after enalapril treatment revealed that enalapril treatment led to enrichment of pSmad1/5/9 in the GO pathway associated with DNA replication, the cell cycle, and the oxidative stress response, all of which are crucial for cell growth (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Genes whose expression increased after enalapril treatment were enriched in pathways related to the response to oxidative stress.
source: Moreover, transcriptome analysis revealed that the genes whose expression increased after enalapril treatment were also enriched in pathways related to the response to oxidative stress (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Genes upregulated by enalapril in response to oxidative stress included antioxidative enzymes, electron transport chain components, and lipid oxidation inhibitors.
source: Notably, genes upregulated by enalapril in response to oxidative stress included antioxidative enzymes, electron transport chain components, and lipid oxidation inhibitors, with a significant increase in pSmad1/5/9 at their TSS regions (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by heatmap and profile plot data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Enalapril treatment increased pSmad1/5/9 enrichment at the promoter regions of antioxidative genes such as PRDX5 and TXN.
source: Specifically, we also examined the promoter regions of antioxidative genes, such as the antioxidative enzyme PRDX5 and the lipid oxidation inhibitor TXN, and found increased pSmad1/5/9 enrichment along with upregulated gene expression (Figure 4D, F–H).
evidence: This is supported by IGV analysis shown in Figure 4F and H, and Western blot data in Figure 4D.

claim: During cellular senescence, a decrease in antioxidative genes exacerbates oxidative stress, reduces energy metabolism, and increases lipid oxidation.
source: During cellular senescence, a decrease in these antioxidative genes exacerbates oxidative stress, reduces energy metabolism, and increases lipid oxidation, leading to the release of inflammatory cytokines (Figure 4E; Coppé et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4E and citation to Coppé et al., 2008.

claim: Cellular senescence increased ROS levels.
source: The results revealed that cellular senescence increased ROS, whereas enalapril slowed the increase in ROS, indicating its ability to upregulate antioxidative genes and reduce ROS, thus affecting cellular senescence (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by DCFH-DA probe measurements shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Enalapril slowed the increase in ROS levels.
source: The results revealed that cellular senescence increased ROS, whereas enalapril slowed the increase in ROS, indicating its ability to upregulate antioxidative genes and reduce ROS, thus affecting cellular senescence (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by DCFH-DA probe measurements shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The continued addition of BMP receptor inhibitors LDN reversed the beneficial effects of enalapril on ROS.
source: Importantly, the continued addition of BMP receptor inhibitors LDN reversed the beneficial effects of enalapril on ROS and decreased pSmad1/5/9 enrichment at the promoters of these antioxidative genes (Figure 4G, I).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4G and ROS measurements in Figure 4I.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of BMPR1A led to decreased expression of antioxidative genes such as PRDX5 and TXN.
source: Similarly, shRNA-mediated knockdown of BMPR1A also led to decreased expression of antioxidative genes such as PRDX5 and TXN (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Enalapril induced organ-specific gene expression changes in six key organs of mice.
source: We found that enalapril induced organ-specific gene expression changes, thereby affecting the physiological functions of these genes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis of brain, kidney, liver, heart, muscle, and spleen.

claim: GSEA revealed upregulated pathways related to forebrain and kidney development, long-chain fatty acid metabolism after enalapril treatment.
source: Moreover, GSEA revealed upregulated pathways related to forebrain and kidney development, long-chain fatty acid metabolism, and other processes, indicating that enalapril has a beneficial effect on organ functions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Enalapril reduced the expression of SASP factors in multiple organs, particularly the CCL, CXCL, and MMP families.
source: Additionally, enalapril reduced the expression of SASP factors in multiple organs, particularly the CCL, CXCL, and MMP families (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq heatmap data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Serum SASP array analysis revealed a decrease in the secretion of certain SASP proteins, such as CCL6, CCL11, CXCL13, IGFBP-1, and MMP3.
source: Serum SASP array analysis also revealed a decrease in the secretion of certain SASP proteins, such as CCL6, CCL11, CXCL13, IGFBP-1, and MMP3, suggesting that enalapril has anti-inflammatory effects in mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by cytokine array analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Enalapril increased pSmad1/5/9 levels in the brain, kidney, and liver of mice.
source: We observed increased pSmad1/5/9 levels, especially in the brain, kidney, and liver, along with upregulated Id1 and antioxidative genes, notably Txn1 and Txn2 (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Enalapril upregulated Id1 and antioxidative genes, notably Txn1 and Txn2, in mouse organs.
source: We observed increased pSmad1/5/9 levels, especially in the brain, kidney, and liver, along with upregulated Id1 and antioxidative genes, notably Txn1 and Txn2 (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Enalapril treatment increased gene expression of BMP signaling and antioxidative stress-related pathways in the brain, kidney, and liver.
source: Further analysis of BMP signaling and antioxidative stress-related pathways in these organs revealed increased gene expression after enalapril treatment, indicating the activation of this pathway (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq heatmap data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Intraperitoneal injection of the BMP inhibitor LDN reversed the effects of enalapril on SASP factor levels in serum.
source: Building on these findings, intraperitoneal injection of the BMP inhibitor LDN reversed the effects of enalapril. Specifically, SASP factor levels in serum, which were reduced by enalapril, were significantly increased. Additionally, the elevated pSmad1/5/9 and antioxidative genes in the brain, kidney, and liver were markedly downregulated upon LDN treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by cytokine array analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Intraperitoneal injection of the BMP inhibitor LDN reversed the effects of enalapril on pSmad1/5/9 and antioxidative genes in the brain, kidney, and liver.
source: Building on these findings, intraperitoneal injection of the BMP inhibitor LDN reversed the effects of enalapril. Specifically, SASP factor levels in serum, which were reduced by enalapril, were significantly increased. Additionally, the elevated pSmad1/5/9 and antioxidative genes in the brain, kidney, and liver were markedly downregulated upon LDN treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Enalapril had no significant effect on body weight in the mice.
source: Notably, enalapril had no significant effect on body weight in the mice, suggesting that the drug has no overt toxic side effects (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Enalapril improved the decrease in age-related mobility, as evidenced by increased grip strength and extended time in the rotarod fatigue experiments.
source: However, enalapril improved the decrease in age-related mobility, as evidenced by increased grip strength and extended time in the rotarod fatigue experiments, suggesting increased muscle strength and endurance (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This is supported by grip strength and rotarod test data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: Enalapril promoted a substantial increase in the rate of spontaneous alternation in the Y-maze test.
source: Enalapril promoted a substantial increase in the rate of spontaneous alternation in the mice, indicating enhanced spatial memory (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by Y-maze test data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Enalapril increased the number of central area crossings in the open-field test, suggesting a reduction in aging-related anxiety.
source: The open-field test, a valuable tool for assessing autonomous and exploratory behaviors in new environments, demonstrated that enalapril increased the number of central area crossings, suggesting a reduction in aging-related anxiety (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This is supported by open-field test data shown in Figure 6F and G.

claim: LDN treatment reversed the improvements in muscle endurance, spatial memory, and reduced anxiety behaviors conferred by enalapril.
source: However, LDN treatment reversed the improvements in muscle endurance, spatial memory, and reduced anxiety behaviors conferred by enalapril (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–F.

claim: The level of creatinine (CREA) was significantly decreased in enalapril-treated mice, indicating potential functional recovery and improvement of renal function.
source: Moreover, the level of creatinine (CREA), a key marker of kidney function, was significantly decreased in enalapril-treated mice, indicating potential functional recovery and improvement of renal function (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by serum creatinine measurements shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was reduced in enalapril-treated mice, indicating a positive cardiac effect.
source: A heart health indicator, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), was also reduced, indicating a positive cardiac effect of enalapril (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is supported by serum LDH measurements shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Following enalapril treatment, the mice presented significant reductions in TG and LDL levels and a noticeable increase in HDL levels.
source: Following enalapril treatment, the mice presented significant reductions in TG and LDL levels and a noticeable increase in HDL levels (Figure 6K–M).
evidence: This is supported by serum lipid measurements shown in Figure 6K-M.

claim: A decrease in β-gal staining was observed in the brain, liver, and spleen of enalapril-treated mice.
source: A decrease in β-gal staining was observed in the brain, liver, and spleen of enalapril-treated mice, suggesting an alleviation of aging-associated phenotypes (Figure 6N, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by SA-β-gal staining data shown in Figure 6N and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: PAS staining revealed a significant reduction in glycogen near the hippocampus after enalapril treatment.
source: Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining, which is indicative of glycogen deposition, revealed a significant reduction in glycogen near the hippocampus (Figure 6O, Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by PAS staining data shown in Figure 6O and Figure 6—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Congo red staining revealed reduced amyloid protein deposition in the cerebral cortex after enalapril treatment.
source: Congo red staining, which detects amyloid protein deposition, also revealed reduced staining in the cerebral cortex (Figure 6P, Figure 6—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by Congo red staining data shown in Figure 6P and Figure 6—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Sirius red staining revealed reduced fibrosis in the kidneys of enalapril-treated mice.
source: In the kidney, Sirius red staining, which highlights abnormal collagen fibers or fibrosis, revealed significant red staining around blood vessels in control mice. However, this staining was noticeably reduced in the kidneys of the mice treated with enalapril (Figure 6Q, Figure 6—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is supported by Sirius red staining data shown in Figure 6Q and Figure 6—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Analysis of spleen, kidney, and liver sections from enalapril-treated mice revealed a reduction in Oil Red O staining.
source: Furthermore, analysis of spleen, kidney, and liver sections from enalapril-treated mice revealed a reduction in Oil Red O staining, with the kidneys and liver showing the most significant changes (Figure 6R, Figure 6—figure supplement 2G–I).
evidence: This is supported by Oil Red O staining data shown in Figure 6R and Figure 6—figure supplement 2G–I.

claim: H&E staining of the liver revealed a decrease in cavities and increased tissue density in mice treated with enalapril.
source: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining of the liver revealed a decrease in cavities and increased tissue density in mice treated with enalapril, suggesting its role in enhancing liver cell proliferation and regeneration (Figure 6S, Figure 6—figure supplement 2J).
evidence: This is supported by H&E staining data shown in Figure 6S and Figure 6—figure supplement 2J.

claim: Enalapril is a commonly prescribed ACE inhibitor for hypertension.
source: In our study, we discovered that enalapril, a commonly prescribed ACE inhibitor for hypertension, has significant anti-senescence effects at both the cellular and organismal levels (Figure 7).
evidence: This is established knowledge about enalapril's clinical use.

claim: Enalapril demonstrated a notable ability to attenuate aging-related physiological decline across multiple organs, including the brain, kidneys, and liver.
source: Enalapril demonstrated a notable ability to attenuate aging-related physiological decline across multiple organs, including the brain, kidneys, and liver.
evidence: This is supported by comprehensive experimental data from behavioral tests, serum analyses, and tissue staining.

claim: Other ACE inhibitors, such as captopril, have been shown to increase longevity in organisms such as C. elegans and mice.
source: This observation aligns with previous reports on the lifespan-extending effects of other ACE inhibitors, such as captopril, which have been shown to increase longevity in organisms such as C. elegans and mice (Egan et al., 2024; Kumar et al., 2016; Strong et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Egan et al., 2024; Kumar et al., 2016; Strong et al., 2022.

claim: Enalapril outperformed captopril and other antihypertensive drugs in ameliorating senescent phenotypes.
source: However, our screening process revealed that enalapril outperformed captopril and other antihypertensive drugs in ameliorating senescent phenotypes, although captopril and other antihypertensive drugs also exhibited the ability to delay senescence.
evidence: This is supported by the drug screening data from the study.

claim: Enalapril enhances the phosphorylation of Smad1/5/9, a critical signaling pathway that regulates various cellular processes, including cell proliferation and the oxidative stress response.
source: Mechanistically, our data revealed that enalapril enhances the phosphorylation of Smad1/5/9, a critical signaling pathway that regulates various cellular processes, including cell proliferation and the oxidative stress response.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot, CUT&Tag, and functional studies with inhibitors.

claim: Phosphorylation of Smad1/5/9 facilitates its nuclear translocation, where it acts as a transcriptional regulator to upregulate downstream genes.
source: Phosphorylation of Smad1/5/9 facilitates its nuclear translocation, where it acts as a transcriptional regulator to upregulate downstream genes, such as those involved in cell cycle regulation and antioxidative responses.
evidence: This is supported by CUT&Tag analysis and established knowledge about Smad signaling.

claim: Rapamycin inhibits the mTOR pathway, which is associated with cell growth and metabolism.
source: For example, rapamycin, which was originally used as an immunosuppressant to prevent organ transplant rejection, inhibits the mTOR pathway, which is associated with cell growth and metabolism (Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2013.

claim: Rapamycin extends the lifespan of mice and shows potential anti-aging effects across various species.
source: It extends the lifespan of mice and shows potential anti-aging effects across various species (Harrison et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harrison et al., 2009.

claim: As an ACE inhibitor, enalapril inherently targets the renin‒angiotensin system, providing vascular protection.
source: As an ACE inhibitor, enalapril inherently targets the renin‒angiotensin system, providing vascular protection (Schmieder et al., 2007; Yamamoto and Rakugi, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schmieder et al., 2007 and Yamamoto and Rakugi, 2021.

claim: Rapamycin may have more pronounced side effects, such as immunosuppression, limiting its long-term use.
source: Compared with repurposed drugs such as rapamycin, which may have more pronounced side effects, such as immunosuppression, limiting their long-term use, enalapril has a well-established safety profile (Janes and Fruman, 2009; Saunders et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Janes and Fruman, 2009 and Saunders et al., 2001.

claim: Enalapril has a well-established safety profile.
source: Compared with repurposed drugs such as rapamycin, which may have more pronounced side effects, such as immunosuppression, limiting their long-term use, enalapril has a well-established safety profile (Janes and Fruman, 2009; Saunders et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Janes and Fruman, 2009 and Saunders et al., 2001, and represents established knowledge.

claim: Enalapril is not uniform across all organs and tissues, as indicated by the differential improvement in aging phenotypes among various tissues.
source: Notably, enalapril is not uniform across all organs and tissues, as indicated by the differential improvement in aging phenotypes among various tissues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed organ-specific effects in the RNA-seq and phenotypic data.

claim: Improvements in metabolic function in the liver could have downstream effects on brain function.
source: Moreover, improvements in metabolic function in the liver could have downstream effects on brain function, as metabolic dysregulation is known to exacerbate neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms based on established knowledge.

claim: Enhanced vascular health resulting from the antihypertensive properties of enalapril may contribute to improved brain perfusion, reducing the risk of age-related cognitive decline.
source: Similarly, enhanced vascular health resulting from the antihypertensive properties of enalapril may contribute to improved brain perfusion, reducing the risk of age-related cognitive decline.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms based on established knowledge.
